title: The Value of Labels in Data Selection for Least Squares
summary:
arXiv:2611.28169v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Suppose a selector sees a finite labelled dataset and chooses $n$ of its rows, with repetition. Ordinary least squares is then fitted to the rows that were chosen, without weights, and the excess loss of the fit on the full dataset is measured in units of the optimal loss. Without further assumptions this ratio does not decay with $n$. We examine the problem for $d$ features and rows of normalized leverage at most $\kappa$, and determine or bound the leading constants. A selector that must establish its rule before seeing the labels has an optimal worst-case ratio of $d\kappa/n$ to leading order, whatever use it makes of the features. With scalar labels, a selector that sees the labels achieves a value between $d\kappa/(2n)$ and $d\kappa\Lambda_d/n$, where $\Lambda_d<1$ is the rounding constant of mean selection. For $d\le4$, the constant is then $d\kappa/2$, so that labels are worth exactly a factor of two there, and for one feature and $m$ outputs it is $\kappa\Lambda_m$. With two or more features the selector can change the proportions of the frequent rows and therefore reshape its own design matrix. We design a simplified optimization problem, which we call a game, that bounds the constant for datasets with exactly fitted frequent rows, then show that its value is at most one half of the gradient energy in several regimes, and that one half is exact along directions in which the frequent rows are rigid, such as an intercept. For grouped designs, in which reshaping amounts to the allocation of a common budget, the constant is $27d/128$ up to an additive constant, compared with $d$ without labels. Nevertheless, one half is not the constant in every dimension: we construct datasets of extremely high dimension and large leverage on which every selection has an excess ratio of at least $(e^{-1/2}-o(1))\,d\kappa/n$, so that labels are worth at most a factor close to $\sqrt e$ there.

event_model_payload.title: The Value of Labels in Data Selection for Least Squares

title: Rollout Scheduling for Chaotic Neural ODEs: Coverage Gains, Computational Cost, and Predictive Accuracy
summary:
arXiv:2611.28192v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Training Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs) on chaotic systems is difficult because small changes in model parameters can lead to rapidly growing differences in predictions. A rollout is a trajectory predicted by the model. Choosing its length from a single global Lyapunov time overlooks differences in local instability. We study rollout scheduling for training on one contiguous rollout per sampled state, asking whether adapting its length to local instability improves prediction. We find the schedule that uses the most trajectory data under an instability budget, a limit on how much instability any one rollout may accumulate. Under stated assumptions, we bound the resulting coverage gain and the coverage lost when the instability estimates are in error. Numerical checks illustrate the theory. Training experiments on Lorenz-63, Lorenz-96, and Kuramoto--Sivashinsky compare adaptive and constant schedules at the same instability budgets and maximum rollout lengths. The budgets are computed from the true system's finite-time Lyapunov exponents. Across the tested settings, adaptive schedules increase trajectory coverage at additional computational cost, without showing a consistent improvement in prediction accuracy. On Lorenz-63, limiting adaptive rollouts to the horizon used to estimate instability improves prediction at the larger budgets. On Kuramoto--Sivashinsky, most configurations provide useful short-time predictions, while all tested long rollouts eventually fail. These findings show why coverage, prediction accuracy, and long-time behavior need separate evaluation, and why instability estimates should be checked over the windows used in training.

event_model_payload.title: Rollout Scheduling for Chaotic Neural ODEs: Coverage Gains, Computational Cost, and Predictive Accuracy

title: Variable Importance Recovery in Tabular Foundation Models: A Simulation Study
summary:
arXiv:2611.28241v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In machine learning, identifying which variables contribute predictive information can be as important as predictive accuracy. Tabular foundation models have matched or exceeded the predictive performance of tuned gradient boosting trees on many small- and medium-sized tabular datasets. Yet their ability to recover population-level variable importance has received little attention. We design and conduct a Monte Carlo simulation study to compare variable importance recovery across tabular foundation models and established machine learning baselines. Our framework distinguishes multiple population estimands, pairs each one with an aligned model-agnostic importance estimator, and evaluates recovery in terms of ranking, support, and relative magnitude. Our results show that tabular foundation models are generally competitive with established machine-learning baselines in recovering population variable importance, and often more accurate. We thus extend the evidence for their capabilities to a previously underexamined dimension, further strengthening their appeal.

title: Directional Bias in Quantile SGD and Score-Inversion Inference under Dependence
summary:
arXiv:2611.28367v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantile stochastic gradient descent (SGD) tracks a quantile by comparing each observation with an adaptive threshold, and closely related updates calibrate online conformal sets and drive quantile temporal-difference learning. Their inputs are serially dependent, yet existing guarantees largely assume independence. We show that dependence creates a directional bias that score autocovariances cannot detect: reversing a stationary stream leaves every score autocovariance unchanged but can change the leading bias threefold. For finite memory and decreasing stepsizes, the bias splits into lag-specific interactions between the threshold and the current observation and a curvature term; delaying the threshold removes the interactions one lag at a time while keeping every observation and the leading variance. At stepsizes near $t^{-1/2}$, as used for online inference, the bias is comparable to the standard error and makes an SGD-based interval miss mostly on one side. Testing fixed candidates instead keeps the score centered, so calibration depends only on score autocovariances. Extending local-dependence self-normalized approximations to the implemented acceptance hull, we show that inverting these tests gives a density-free, moment-free interval for the population quantile with $O(n^{-1/2})$ coverage error for a fixed sufficient lag window, a rate that is sharp for this interval, and a guarantee for data-selected windows; an exact scan takes $O(n\log n)$ time. Experiments confirm the lag-by-lag predictions and show calibration competitive with block bootstrap at lower cost.

event_model_payload.title: Directional Bias in Quantile SGD and Score-Inversion Inference under Dependence

title: Beyond Gaussian Calibration: Local Inference in Decentralized SGD
summary:
arXiv:2611.28370v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Decentralized SGD minimizes a common objective by local gradient steps and neighbor averaging. Its statistical theory mostly concerns network averages, yet clients act on their own iterates, and one-sided decisions such as alarms use one tail of the local error. We show that a client's constant-step endpoint can have nearly nominal Gaussian coverage while both tails are badly miscalibrated. An exact noise-filter representation explains why: a quantity computable from the graph and stepsize decides whether the endpoint is asymptotically Gaussian, and when the number of clients outgrows the inverse stepsize on networks with summable return probabilities, such as lazy tori of dimension at least three and expanders, a few recent noise terms at nearby clients keep a fixed share of local variance. On these tori the limit is a non-Gaussian local field plus an independent Gaussian consensus term, and no reference distribution built from finitely many noise moments, including Edgeworth and Cornish--Fisher corrections, is calibrated at all levels uniformly over noise laws. We propose a hybrid reference that resamples the influential noise terms from their empirical law and replaces the rest by a Gaussian; its non-asymptotic coverage bound allows noise laws and curvature estimated from fresh gradients or the client's trajectory, and extends to nonlinear vector objectives. In full-network simulations it restores tail balance at essentially unchanged interval length, also under rare large shocks that break Cornish--Fisher intervals; gains vanish, as predicted, when consensus dominates.

event_model_payload.title: Beyond Gaussian Calibration: Local Inference in Decentralized SGD

title: Targeted Learning for Externally Controlled Trials and Beyond
summary:
arXiv:2611.28421v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper focuses on externally controlled trials (ECTs), which consist of a single-arm clinical trial supplemented by an external control arm (ECA). Potential data sources for the ECA can be broadly classified into three categories: (i) the control arm of a historical clinical trial, (ii) a concurrent cohort study, and (iii) external real-world data (RWD). In this paper, we consider a broad class of estimands defined through balancing weights. For a given estimand in the class, we discuss the efficient influence function (EIF) and the targeted maximum likelihood estimator (TMLE), together with practical implementation algorithms. Within the targeted learning framework, TMLE is a substitution estimator that enjoys several desirable theoretical properties and favorable finite-sample performance. Finally, the proposed framework is extended to two additional settings: (1) randomized controlled trials (RCTs) augmented with external covariate information to define a target population, and (2) indirect treatment comparisons (ITCs) that combine individual patient data (IPD) from an internal RCT with aggregate data (AgD) from an external RCT.

event_model_payload.title: Targeted Learning for Externally Controlled Trials and Beyond

title: Guidance-Induced Activation of Score Estimation Errors in Diffusion Models
summary:
arXiv:2611.28451v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines conditional and unconditional score estimates to steer diffusion sampling. The weighted-solenoidal component of each score error has no instantaneous effect on the evolution of its corresponding reference density. Because the guided density in CFG generally differs from both reference densities, the combination of these solenoidal components can affect the evolution of the guided marginals. We call this mechanism guidance-induced error activation. Using a weighted Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition, we identify the activated error field, quantify its magnitude, and characterize when it vanishes. At fixed noise time, the activated error field varies continuously with guidance strength. Its weak first-order variation has two terms, one from reweighting the errors and one from the change in the guided density. For finite score errors, ODE characteristics and an SDE Feynman-Kac formula connect error-activation to the generated densities. For a class of finite Gaussian mixtures, error-activation can account for most of the KL divergence between the generated distributions by learned-score and exact-score CFG ODE samplers under strong guidance. Ideal score filtering removes the weighted-solenoidal errors and eliminates error-activation. Controlled experiments with Gaussian and Gamma mixtures illustrate how activation affects the generated densities. Qualitative CIFAR-10 comparisons suggest that filtering can help preserve object structure under strong guidance.

event_model_payload.title: Guidance-Induced Activation of Score Estimation Errors in Diffusion Models

title: A hybrid Graph-based Machine Learning Model for predicting Delivery Times in Supply Chain Logistics
summary:
arXiv:2611.28467v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Global supply chains are increasingly vulnerable to disruptions arising from external events, such as natural disasters and geopolitical crises, and from internal operational inefficiencies, including supplier delays and bottlenecks in order shipping. This work, conducted within the Horizon Europe project M4ESTRO, introduces a hybrid modelling approach combining graph theory and machine learning to represent supply chain logistics operations, with a focus on predicting delays in inbound flows between industrial suppliers and manufacturing entities. The various stages of order fulfilment are modelled through a formal mathematical framework, by defining disruption indicators computed from both historical and real-time data drawn from heterogeneous sources, including traffic and weather conditions and supplier dispatch readiness. Building on a graph-based representation of the supply chain, stochastic methods based on Markov chains are applied to estimate delivery times, detect schedule deviations, quantify prediction uncertainty, and produce interpretable metrics to support operational decision-making. Within the M4ESTRO project, the proposed framework was applied to build a web application for real-time tracking of inbound logistics, and was validated in a use case with an industrial project partner. The web application successfully enabled early detection of logistics disruptions along the supply chain and provided stakeholders with the visibility needed to act before delays propagated. The underlying model proved effective as the basis of a resilient, data-driven logistics tracking system, aligned with the digital transformation objectives of industry and with Manufacturing-as-a-Service paradigms.

event_model_payload.title: A hybrid Graph-based Machine Learning Model for predicting Delivery Times in Supply Chain Logistics

title: When and Where to Transfer: Learning Transferable Historical Contexts for Short-History Multivariate Time Series Forecasting
summary:
arXiv:2611.28567v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Related sources can improve multivariate time series forecasting when the target history is short, but their usefulness varies across source groups and historical periods. A key challenge is to identify informative historical contexts from the sources. This paper proposes Hierarchical Context Transfer (HiCT), a framework that adaptively weights source groups and their historical contexts to determine both \emph{where} and \emph{when} to transfer. A shared context encoder and cross-attention are used to learn weights over source groups and historical contexts. These weights guide regularized transfer estimation, followed by an optional target-specific correction. This paper establishes a target excess-risk bound for the context-weighted transfer estimator. Experiments demonstrate competitive predictive performance across four multivariate forecasting datasets and a favorable accuracy--runtime trade-off against the evaluated baselines. Source-corruption ablations illustrate the roles of group-level and within-group weighting in adapting to unreliable source histories.

title: Complex band-limited maximum likelihood: estimating the wave behind detected quanta
summary:
arXiv:2611.28572v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Detected photons and electrons land at positions drawn from $|\psi|^2$, yet it is $\psi$, phase included, that a wave equation propagates, and the state that produced the particles is often known only in part. A density estimator can recover $|\psi|^2$ directly from the positions, without any wave equation, but it discards the phase, and with it the state. We introduce complex band-limited maximum likelihood (complex BLML), which estimates $\psi$ itself by maximising the likelihood of the detected positions over exactly the intensities the physics allows: squared moduli of complex functions whose spectrum lies in a given set, such as a band, the shape of the aperture, or several modes for a partially coherent source. A single eigenvalue can certify a global maximum. On simulated two-slit far fields we measure what each prior is worth: a band reaches a given accuracy with seven times fewer photons than a kernel density estimate and already gives the fringe contrast and the relative phase, and the shape of the aperture adds the slit geometry. Some quantities need a prior at any number of photons: for slits of one profile the intensity fixes only the contrast $2\rho V/(1+\rho^2)$, and on a line two different apertures can produce the same particles. Cutting a pattern to a few fringes, as published records are, removes the slit width. On four public single-particle double-slit records it predicts held-out particles best among the methods we tested, kernel estimators and two-slit optical models included, and it recovers the fringe contrast without a model of the optics. On fluorescent beads it finds the resolution limit of the microscope, $2\mathrm{NA}/\lambda$, from the photons alone.

title: A Novel Approach to Clustering Shape Data Using Iteratively Weighted Vectors with k-Means
summary:
arXiv:2611.28880v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Topological data analysis provides a collection of methods for analyzing data with shape structure, including point clouds, graphs, and images. Recent advances in topological vectorization have enabled the embedding of shape data into Euclidean spaces, facilitating comparisons and machine learning tasks. Vector summaries that effectively capture topological structures are particularly useful for shape classification and unsupervised learning tasks such as clustering. We investigate the use of vectorized topological data for clustering through k-means, which partitions observations into a fixed number of groups by minimizing a squared-error loss function. By incorporating an element-wise weight-update step into the iterative k-means algorithm, we improve clustering performance on both simulated and real-world shape datasets. We show that estimating these weights reduces to a least-squares problem, requiring minimal additional computation while allowing flexible coefficient constraints. Our approach also substantially strengthens the negative correlation between the loss and clustering accuracy, improving the effectiveness of selecting among multiple clustering solutions based on the lowest loss. These improvements remain robust to changes in vector length and the number of initializations. Furthermore, weighted topological vector summaries exhibit stability under small structural perturbations, particularly when weight constraints are imposed. The proposed method offers a flexible alternative for clustering topological data, accommodating different k-means variants, vectorization methods, and weight constraints.

event_model_payload.title: A Novel Approach to Clustering Shape Data Using Iteratively Weighted Vectors with k-Means

title: A comparison of knot point screening algorithms for highly adaptive lasso
summary:
arXiv:2611.29270v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Highly adaptive lasso (HAL) is a nonparametric regression estimator with a rate of convergence $n^{-1/3}(\log n)^{d/2}$, where the data dimension $d$ only appears in the power of the log of sample size. This fast rate is crucial for many causal inference tasks, where efficient estimation typically requires nuisance parameters to be estimated at a specific rate. HAL achieves this rate and, when paired with semiparametrically efficient estimators -- such as those constructed using targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) -- can be used to develop efficient estimators. Beyond causal inference, HAL is applicable to a wide range of supervised machine learning tasks. The procedure for HAL involves first performing a basis expansion on the original design matrix $X$ and then computing a lasso solution path. Cross-validation is used to select the optimal $L_1$-norm for the coefficients. For datasets with all continuous covariates and no ties, the HAL design matrix can reach a dimension as large as $n \times n(2^d-1)$, imposing a significant computational and memory burden. To address this, screening algorithms are applied at both the variable and knot-point levels to make HAL practical for datasets of moderate to large sizes. In this work, we propose outcome-blind knot point screening based on center-based clustering -- $k$-means and partitioning around medoids (PAM) -- and compare it with the quantile-based screening implemented in the hal9001 R package at matched design-matrix sizes. Across 153 simulation settings, $k$-means and PAM significantly improved test $R^2$ in 97 and 111 settings, respectively, with gains that grow with covariate skewness, while producing slightly smaller design matrices. On nine real-world datasets, they reduced the cross-validated mean squared error by 35-36% on the dataset with the most skewed predictors and performed comparably on the others.

title: Optimal Labelling Designs for Sequential Decisions on Language Model Updates
summary:
arXiv:2611.29416v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: When a large language model (LLM) is updated, its developer must decide whether accuracy improved, worsened or stayed within a tolerance. An LLM judge can assess every prompt cheaply but imperfectly, while human labels are costly. We propose Sequential Decisions with Optimal Labelling Designs (SOLD), which labels one prompt at a time, uses the judge to correct the estimate of the change in accuracy and to choose the prompts, and stops once the evidence is conclusive. A wrong decision has probability at most a prespecified level whenever labelling stops. The commonly used Neyman allocation minimises the variance of the estimate and therefore rarely labels prompts that the judge is confident about. It can need far more draws when the outcomes of these prompts could still fall far below the judge's prediction. We instead derive the design that gathers evidence fastest, which labels each prompt with probability at least proportional to how far its outcome could fall below the prediction. As the level tends to zero, no procedure based on the judge-corrected estimates needs fewer draws than SOLD. In simulations and on the EVOUNA and MMLU-Pro datasets, SOLD needed fewer labels than the other methods.

event_model_payload.title: Optimal Labelling Designs for Sequential Decisions on Language Model Updates

title: Tabular Foundation Models for Weighted Regression and Classification
summary:
arXiv:2611.29789v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Weighted regression and classification have applications ranging from missing-data analysis and causal inference to insurance pricing and particle physics. Existing weighted methods must be fitted and tuned on each dataset, which is costly for flexible nonlinear learners. Tabular foundation models avoid this cost. A Transformer is pretrained once on many simulated datasets and then predicts on a new dataset by in-context learning, using its observations as context without further fitting. Recent models such as TabPFN-3.5 surpass tuned conventional methods, but they cannot use sample weights. We develop a general pipeline that adapts such models to weighted prediction through weighted attention, a normalized weighted loss, and pretraining on synthetic weighted prediction tasks from missing-data problems. Applied to TabPFN-3.5, it yields WeightedPFN, which performs strongly on real datasets, both in missing-data problems and in out-of-distribution causal tasks, while running about as fast as linear baselines. We also establish a statistical theory showing that a suitably pretrained weighted Transformer attains the nonparametric minimax rate for weighted regression on new datasets without further fitting.

title: Wavelet determinantal samplers: Optimal approximation rates adapting to regularity
summary:
arXiv:2611.29992v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We construct wavelet-based determinantal samplers on manifolds and geometric graphs whose approximation rates adapt to the regularity of the observable. On a Riemannian manifold of dimension $m$, our wavelet DPPs satisfy variance reduction of order $n^{1-2s/m}$ for linear statistics of both $s$-H\"older and $H^s$ observables, where $0<s\le1$. Using these samplers, we further construct unbiased quadrature rules with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$ using at most $3n/2$ function evaluations, matching the classical optimal randomized integration exponent. For point clouds sampled from an $m$-dimensional manifold, we develop corresponding determinantal samplers on two standard classes of geometric random graphs: $\varepsilon$-graphs and symmetric $k$-nearest-neighbour graphs. These samplers satisfy the same variance reduction for linear statistics of $s$-H\"older observables and yield conditionally unbiased estimators of empirical averages with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$, using at most $2n$ function evaluations. In both settings, the rates are governed by the intrinsic dimension $m$ and the regularity $s$ of the observable.

title: Statistically Optimal and Near Linear Time Hypothesis Selection
summary:
arXiv:2611.30003v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In hypothesis selection we are given $n$ distributions $q_1,\dots,q_n$ on a countable domain $\mathcal{X}$ and samples from an unknown distribution $p$. The goal is a distribution $q$ with $\mathrm{TV}(p,q)\le\alpha\min_i\mathrm{TV}(p,q_i)+\epsilon$. The factor $\alpha=2$ is optimal for algorithms using a number of samples from $p$ that is independent of $|\mathcal{X}|$, and in general only improper learners achieve it. We give a learner that achieves $\alpha=2$ with $O(\log(n/\delta)/\epsilon^2)$ samples of $p$, with probability at least $1-\delta$. This matches the sample complexity of Yatracos's factor-$3$ estimator, and it removes the logarithmic factors in the factor-$2$ bound of Bousquet et al. (FOCS 2021). The learner accesses the $q_i$ only through sampling and pointwise comparisons. We measure its running time by its oracle complexity, the number of oracle calls. In expectation it makes $O((n\epsilon^{-2}+\epsilon^{-4}\log(1/\epsilon))\log(n/\delta))$ oracle calls, independent of $\mathcal{X}$. It runs multiplicative weights over the constraints $\mathrm{TV}(q,q_i)\le\mathrm{TV}(p,q_i)$ and uses at most one sample of $p$ per round.

title: Sequential Selection against an Adaptive Opponent
summary:
arXiv:2611.30006v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Selecting a strategy by testing it against an opponent is common in game-playing AI, red-teaming of language models, and safety evaluations of AI agents. In many of these settings, the opponent adapts to what it observes, so a strategy that keeps winning in practice may already have stopped working by the time it is used. Motivated by these settings, we study a player who tries strategies in practice games against an adaptive opponent, decides when to stop, and then either selects one strategy for the next game or abstains. The goal is to select a strategy that meets a target win probability while rarely selecting one that has already fallen below it. For a single strategy, we propose the Sequential Private Accumulated-excess Rule (SPAR), which accumulates evidence through a capped likelihood ratio and selects the strategy once this evidence reaches a privately drawn uniform threshold. We show that the stopping time must involve such private randomness. The number of games SPAR needs is inversely proportional to the error tolerance, and this rate is optimal even when the opponent happens not to adapt. To select among multiple strategies, we introduce Screen-then-SPAR, which screens candidates in stages before applying SPAR. The procedure adapts to the best strategy's unknown initial margin above the target and achieves the minimax rate up to logarithmic factors. The performance of Screen-then-SPAR is demonstrated through simulations and two real-data studies, one using recorded coding-agent attacks from MonitoringBench and the other using rock-paper-scissors matches between human players and an adaptive bot.

event_model_payload.title: Sequential Selection against an Adaptive Opponent

title: The response field approach to path integral control
summary:
arXiv:2611.30044v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This paper investigates non-linear path integral control problems within the response field formalism of nonequilibrium field theory. The aim of this work is exploratory, based on the identification of correspondences between backward adjoint processes and the response field of non-equilibrium statistical physics, whose properties have not been set out in an optimal control setting. The response field is found to play an analogous role to the backward adjoint process under the stochastic maximum principle. In particular, the gradient of the optimal cost-to-go at the initial time, which is proportional to the optimal control, is given by the average of the response field at the initial time. In contrast to the case of non-equilibrium dynamics, the response function is found to be acausal in the control setting. The linear-quadratic case of path integral control is studied, confirming it as the free theory, meaning that solving the control problem is equivalent to completing the square and determining the propagator for a two point boundary value problem. The developments presented here are a necessary prelude to applications based on field theoretic approximation, for both path integral control and their dual inference problems.

title: Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization: Fine-Tuning Language Models toward Alignment beyond Transitive Preferences
summary:
arXiv:2611.30135v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The growing adoption of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which leverages pairwise preference data, reflects its great success in fine-tuning large language models to align with human expectations. It directly optimizes the policy from human preferences without explicit reward modeling or the complexities of reinforcement learning-based approaches. However, the classic DPO relies on the Bradley--Terry sampling model and cannot effectively capture intransitivity or cyclic structures in aggregated human preference data. In this article, we propose Sparse Hodge Preference Optimization (SHPO), a preference optimization algorithm that augments DPO with a sparse antisymmetric curl residual motivated by the combinatorial Hodge decomposition. We prove that SHPO strictly enlarges DPO's hypothesis class on comparison graphs containing at least one triangle, under some mild regularity conditions on the response representations. We further establish a theoretical guarantee for $\ell_1$-regularized estimation of the curl coefficients under fixed policy and representations. Qualitative studies on three preference datasets under the same QLoRA budget, SHPO-aligned LLM achieves satisfactory performances in preference accuracy, cyclic structure recovery, and GPT-4o-judged generation quality.

title: Tensor Recovery with Heterogeneous Mode Structures
summary:
arXiv:2611.30435v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tensor recovery methods often impose a common structural assumption across modes, even when different modes may exhibit distinct forms of regularity. We propose a unified convex framework that treats each mode according to its structure. Smoothly varying modes form an indexing domain and are handled by local kernel weighting, whereas retained modes may receive low-rank, group-sparse, graph-Laplacian, or autoregressive regularization in distinct and potentially overlapping combinations. The framework also covers ordinary tensor recovery without local smoothing. A consensus HM-ADMM algorithm separates the active penalties into tractable proximal and linear-system updates. For the population-quadratic estimator, we derive deterministic oracle inequalities and high-probability bounds under independent trace regression. The bounds disentangle stochastic error, rank and support complexity, smoothing bias, and quadratic mismatch. They also identify when quadratic penalties sharpen the Frobenius-error bound. For regular smooth domains, the theory characterizes the bias-variance trade-off and yields an optimal bandwidth order, with a specialization to uniform tensor completion. Simulations and two applications illustrate the gains from matching regularization to mode-specific structure, especially under severe undersampling.

title: SCAN: Neural Additive Networks for Scalable High-Order Component Selection and Estimation
summary:
arXiv:2611.30452v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Functional ANOVA models express a prediction as a sum of main effects and interactions, but existing neural functional ANOVA models require the interactions to be specified in advance, which forces a trade-off between missing higher-order structure and the cost of enumerating many interactions. We propose SCAN (Scalable Component Additive Networks), which learns which features each basis function combines, so that components of different orders are selected and estimated jointly without enumerating candidates. The learned component index sets form a small candidate collection on which post-hoc identification is carried out efficiently. A global component-selection parameter shares information across basis functions, and truncating negligible component-selection weights gives a sparse model that is identified after training. We establish universal approximation, a minimax optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor, and component selection consistency, which together imply that the discovered components contain all identified true components with probability tending to one. In synthetic experiments, SCAN learns components whose maximum order is close to the true one, and recovers higher-order components more accurately than the baseline models, with post-hoc identification taking a few seconds for 100 inputs. SCAN also outperforms most neural functional ANOVA models in prediction on the benchmark datasets and trains at a much lower cost than exhaustive second-order models. We also apply SCAN to predict treatment response in breast cancer from 12,502 gene-expression variables.

event_model_payload.title: SCAN: Neural Additive Networks for Scalable High-Order Component Selection and Estimation

title: Precise Asymptotics of Non-Convex M-Estimators
summary:
arXiv:2611.30798v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Precise asymptotic theory for M-estimators in high-dimensional settings is largely limited to convex or mildly non-convex formulations, yet non-convex loss functions as well as regularizers are widely used in practice. We study M-estimation in generalized linear models (GLMs) where the loss function or the regularizer can be non-convex. Under rotationally invariant design matrices in the proportional asymptotic regime, we analyze the problem through Vector Approximate Message Passing (VAMP), whose iterates are described by a low-dimensional deterministic recursion called State Evolution (SE). Existing proofs of SE require the proximal operators of the loss function and the regularizer to be Lipschitz, but a non-convex loss or regularizer can have a discontinuous proximal operator, and the usual Onsager terms in VAMP then miss the contribution of the discontinuities. Assuming that the proximal operators are special functions of locally bounded variation, we derive a correction to the Onsager terms using a distributional Stein's lemma. We prove that SE holds for the corrected VAMP. We apply the theory to analyze group sparse regression with an $\ell_0$-type penalty and to robust regression with the Cauchy loss.

title: Fast and Consistent Structure Learning in Graphical Models via Approximate Cross-Validation
summary:
arXiv:2611.30822v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Structure learning for sparse graphical models in high dimensions requires both computational scalability and selection consistency. Classical criteria such as (Extended) Bayesian Information Criterion can provide consistency, but rely on model-specific likelihoods and complexity calibration. In comparison, cross-validation avoids such analytic calibration and is therefore attractive for graph learning. However, cross-validation is computationally infeasible and theoretically inconsistent in structure learning. This creates a tension between consistency and flexibility in modeling. In this work, we resolve the tension by developing a scalable graph-recovery procedure built on approximate cross-validation. We demonstrate its effectiveness in learning large graphical models both theoretically and empirically, and establish selection consistency under mild signal strength assumptions.

event_model_payload.title: Fast and Consistent Structure Learning in Graphical Models via Approximate Cross-Validation

title: A theory of inductive node-level generalization from a single large graph
summary:
arXiv:2611.30937v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In Graph Machine Learning (GML), the notion of generalization fundamentally varies depending on the task level and the properties of the dataset. For instance, graph-level tasks fit into the traditional ML framework of i.i.d. samples, with relatively small graphs. On the contrary, node-level tasks involve dependent nodes, often in a few large graphs. Existing studies often consider the transductive settings, where training and test data co-exist in the same graph, or, for inductive learning, try to recover some kind of probabilistic ``independence'', e.g. by still assuming a large number of independent graphs or subgraphs.
  In this work, we develop a novel framework to express the generalization capabilities of Graph ML algorithms for inductive node-level tasks when learning from a single large graph, taking inspiration from the literature on GNN transferability. In particular, we emphasize the similarities with classical ML by revisiting the excess risk decomposition with a new notion of ``transferable'' risk on large graphs. We apply this framework to Latent Position random graphs: we uncover new insights on the hardness of GML compared to traditional ML, and derive novel notions of concentration. Finally, we apply this framework to several models of GNNs, unifying several existing results on GNNs transferability and universality.

event_model_payload.title: A theory of inductive node-level generalization from a single large graph

title: Prediction-Powered Regression via Calibration: Beyond the Supervised Minimax Benchmark
summary:
arXiv:2611.30976v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study nonparametric regression with limited labeled data and abundant observations carrying potentially inaccurate pseudo-labels. Our proposed method, weighted prediction-powered regression via calibration (wPPRC), first calibrates pseudo-labels using labeled data, then fits a predictor by weighted regression using observed and calibrated responses. Over H\"older classes, we derive nonasymptotic excess-risk bounds for clipped ReLU estimators and establish a minimax lower bound for the corresponding regression problem. Under suitable conditions, the upper and lower bounds match up to logarithmic factors. Moreover, wPPRC can achieve a worst-case risk of smaller order than the minimax risks under four baseline observation structures on the same joint distribution class, demonstrating the value of additional pseudo-labels. We also construct a validation-selected (VS) estimator using an independent labeled validation sample to choose the weight. The VS estimator satisfies an expected-risk oracle inequality and preserves the improvement over the baseline minimax risks with the same total labeled-data budget. Simulations and an application to predicting homeless counts illustrate the gains of the proposed estimators.

title: Revealing Geometry under Strong Noise: Spectral Embeddings and Clustering via Random Geometric Graphs
summary:
arXiv:2611.31047v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modern massive datasets often contain useful low-dimensional nonlinear structures that are hidden by noise. Spectral embedding algorithms rely on meaningful local relationships between observations, but noise accumulated across many coordinates can make the observed distances unreliable. This also complicates clustering when groups have curved or concentric shapes and cannot be distinguished by their centers. In this paper, we develop a new method that denoises pairwise distances before using them to construct spectral embeddings and identify communities. Our approach uses cross-fitted projections to estimate distances between the underlying signals, selects a neighborhood radius from the observed sample, and builds a random geometric graph whose spectral coordinates represent the latent geometric structure. By connecting nearby points, such a geometric graph can distinguish different groups even when their centers coincide. A novel recursive procedure is then proposed to extract clusters from the graph using its spectral embeddings when such clusters exist.
  On the theoretical side, under a manifold model, we provide guarantees for our spectral embedding algorithm, which can be understood through the eigendecomposition of an integral operator associated with the underlying geometry. We show that the algorithm is robust to noise when the total noise energy is comparable to the total signal energy or, under additional conditions, exceeds it. To our knowledge, this is among the first spectral embedding algorithms that can handle such strong noise in datasets with nonlinear structures. In addition, our proposed clustering algorithm can recover the underlying clusters even when their centers coincide. Numerical studies demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed method in mitigating noise and revealing geometric structures for both spectral embedding and clustering.

event_model_payload.title: Revealing Geometry under Strong Noise: Spectral Embeddings and Clustering via Random Geometric Graphs

title: Learning the Projection onto the Data Support: Distribution Learning that Avoids Memorization
summary:
arXiv:2611.28234v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We introduce a framework for learning distributions supported on manifolds based on estimating the nearest-point projection onto the data support. Specifically, we define an objective functional over a class of functions whose minimizer recovers this projection. The proposed framework automatically adapts to the intrinsic dimension and allows for data supported on unions of manifolds with varying dimensions. The resulting objective can be optimized using standard neural network architectures. We present population-level results establishing recovery of the manifold projection and prove finite-sample Wasserstein generalization bounds. Furthermore, we validate the approach empirically across a range of settings. In contrast to widely used generative models such as diffusion models, whose objectives can be minimized by memorizing training samples, our formulation excludes such behavior. We also introduce a direct memorization metric to verify that the learned projection generates new samples rather than reproducing the training set.

event_model_payload.title: Learning the Projection onto the Data Support: Distribution Learning that Avoids Memorization

title: Which Loans, Not How Many: Exactly Level-Invariant, Anytime-Valid Monitoring of Deployed Risk Models
summary:
arXiv:2611.28342v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: A refinancing wave can change the number of mortgage prepayments without changing the relationship between scores and prepayment. In a logistic model, conditioning on the monthly count removes the intercept from the likelihood of which loans prepay. Our fixed-start slope product tests a lower bound on the calibration slope. At threshold 20 its probability of ever crossing under the null is at most 5%. The restarted level sum tracks departures from intercept tolerance. A confidence sequence estimates a constant slope, and the restart-intersection rule detects changes in that slope. A continuous mixture avoids the off-grid width floor of a discrete prior. On Freddie Mac loans, fixed-slope resampling reproduces 78% of maintained-model monthly AUC variance in development and 70% in the holdout (95% intervals 57-100% and 48-100%). From fresh holdout starts, the restarted level sum crosses on both paths, and the fixed-start slope product stays below threshold on both. The restart-intersection rule signals a downward change for the frozen model in April 2018 and an upward change for the maintained model in a supplementary run in August 2019.

title: Data-Dependent Probability Estimation via Sample Amplification
summary:
arXiv:2611.28399v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Can we estimate the probability of an event chosen after seeing the data, without using any fresh samples? Its empirical probability can be arbitrarily misleading, while learning the entire distribution to constant accuracy requires $\Theta(d)$ samples on a domain of size $d$. We show that $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d})$ samples suffice for constant mean squared error, provided the rule choosing the event is known. More generally, our estimator handles arbitrary $[0,1]$-valued queries and runs in polynomial time given evaluation access to the rule. This sample complexity matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors and resolves the open question posed by Feldman, Kale, Raman, Talwar, and Tewari (arXiv:2610.41244).
  Our estimation framework relies on a new combination of sample amplification (arXiv:1904.12053 and arXiv:2201.04315) with distribution learning via online optimization. Our estimator achieves mean squared error $O(d^{3/4}/n)$ when $d\leq n$ and $\widetilde{O}(d^{1/4}/\sqrt{n})$ when $d>n$. We complement this with a lower bound of $\Omega(\min\{1,\sqrt{d}/n\})$ on the mean squared error. Using our framework, we also design an efficient estimator for data-dependent queries on Gaussian distributions with unknown mean and identity covariance. Finally, we show that a smoothed variant of the problem is much (exponentially) easier. For discrete distributions, if the sample size is chosen uniformly from $\{n,\ldots,2n-1\}$, then $n=O(\log d)$ suffices for constant mean squared error.

event_model_payload.title: Data-Dependent Probability Estimation via Sample Amplification

title: Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections
summary:
arXiv:2611.28579v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We study the sequential prediction problem introduced by Goel et al. (2023), where an adversary can inject arbitrarily many corrupted instances in an i.i.d. stream from a clean distribution $\mu$, while the learner is allowed to abstain from making a prediction at no cost if the current instance was indeed injected. When $\mu$ is unknown, Yu and Blanchard (2026) show a polynomial tradeoff between mistakes and false abstentions for classes with finite VC dimension and oblivious adversaries, but still leave open a significant gap between upper and lower bounds in their tradeoff landscape. In this paper, we propose the weighted shattering potential, and based on variants of this potential, provide gap-closing algorithms that essentially characterize the tradeoffs under various settings of interest: When $\mu$ is known, our algorithm improves over Goel et al. (2023) and achieves their conjectured $O(d\log T)$ mistake bound; When $\mu$ is unknown, for oblivious adversary, our guarantees are tight both in $T$ and in terms of the VC dimension $d$, which completely characterizes the abstention-mistake tradeoff in this setting and gives an $O(\sqrt{dT})$ balanced rate. For adaptive adversary, our results are tight up to $\operatorname{poly}(dD\log T)$ factors for structured classes with finite so-called reduction dimension $D$. Our guarantees also extend to censored feedback, where the label is hidden after an abstention.

event_model_payload.title: Tight Mistake-Abstention Tradeoffs for Sequential Prediction under Adversarial Injections
